headline: Put a copy of a message's algorithm identifiers where its signature or its MAC covers them, and refuse one whose copy disagrees.
summary: A CMS signature covers the algorithms it uses only indirectly, and an authenticated-data message does not cover them at all: RFC 5652 makes the MAC input the authenticated attributes alone, so the digest and MAC algorithm identifiers sit outside it. Rewriting the digest algorithm there leaves the MAC verifying and has the recipient recompute the content digest under the algorithm the attacker chose, which needs no key. `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` now emit the RFC 6211 CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute on request, a copy of those identifiers placed where the signature or the MAC covers them, and `pki.cms.verify` and `pki.cms.decrypt` compare every copy they find against the fields it protects. A disagreement is a refusal, which RFC 6211 requires of any verifier that reads the attribute at all.

Added: `algorithmProtection` on `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` emits the RFC 6211 `CMSAlgorithmProtection` attribute: a copy of the structure's digest algorithm identifier plus its signature algorithm identifier for a `SignerInfo` or its MAC algorithm identifier for an `AuthenticatedData`, each copied whole with its parameters from the value the field itself is built from. RFC 8933 section 4.1 makes including it a SHOULD, and RFC 9882 section 4 and RFC 9814 section 5 repeat that for ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, whose signatures carry no digest identifier of their own. It is off by default, because turning it on changes the bytes of every signature a caller emits. `true` writes the identifier RFC 6211 section 2 and Appendix A state, which OpenSSL registers as `id-aa-CMSAlgorithmProtection` and Bouncy Castle uses; `"registry"` writes the S/MIME arc value the IANA registry and `draft-ietf-lamps-rfc6211-update` give it.

`pki.cms.verify` compares the attribute against the fields it protects on every signer and every countersignature, and reports `algorithmProtection` per signer: `{ present, oid, compared, mismatch }`, where `compared` lists the identifiers actually checked. Both identifiers the attribute is assigned are read, because a verifier that recognizes one spelling and not the other checks nothing on a message using the other, which is the interop failure the update draft records between two shipped implementations. A disagreement fails the signer with `cms/algorithm-protection-mismatch`: section 3.1 makes both comparisons MUSTs once a validator supports the attribute. The digest arm reads absent and DER NULL parameters as one algorithm, which RFC 3370 section 2.1 and RFC 5754 section 2 require an implementation to accept; the signature arm compares the parameters as they are, since that is where RSASSA-PSS keeps its hash, mask generator, salt length and trailer field and the signature covers none of them. `requireAlgorithmProtection` turns an absent attribute into a failure for an operator whose profile asks for one, on every signer and on every countersignature at any depth.

`pki.cms.decrypt` compares the attribute on an `AuthenticatedData`, against the outer `digestAlgorithm` and `macAlgorithm` the MAC input does not cover, and reports the same `algorithmProtection` field on its result. The comparison runs before the MAC, because a mismatch is a statement about the message rather than about the key. `requireAlgorithmProtection` applies here too.

`pki.schema.cms.parseAlgorithmProtection(der)` decodes a `CMSAlgorithmProtection` value held on its own. A value carrying both arms, or neither, is refused `cms/bad-algorithm-protection-attr`, which is section 2's rule that exactly one of them is present; each failure says which. `pki.schema.cms.parse` decodes the attribute during its own walk, so a message carrying a malformed one, more than one value, more than one instance, or an instance in an unsigned, unauthenticated or unprotected position is refused there.

`pki.lint.cms` reports `lint/rfc8933/algorithm-protection-absent` as a notice on a signer that carries signed attributes and no such attribute. The SHOULD is conditioned on signed attributes being present, so a signer that signs the content directly draws nothing.
Changed: Every verb that emits attributes refuses a caller-supplied algorithm protection attribute that this package's own verifier would then reject, with `cms/bad-input`. `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` refuse a copy contradicting the identifiers being emitted, a copy carrying more than one value, and a second one beside the attribute the verb itself emitted; caller-supplied attributes otherwise reach the wire unread. A copy that agrees is admitted. The attribute is refused in `unsignedAttributes`, which RFC 6211 section 2 forbids outright, and in an `AuthEnvelopedData`'s authenticated attributes, which RFC 8933 section 6 says it protects nothing in: that content type has no digest or MAC algorithm field for a copy to name. Asking for `algorithmProtection` together with `signedAttributes: false` is also refused, since the attribute rides in the signed attributes and a message cannot carry it without them.
A verified countersignature row carries one more field, `algorithmProtection`, beside `ok`, `sid`, `cert`, `digestAlgorithm`, `unsignedAttrs` and `countersignatures`.
